content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has conducted extensive evaluations of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine, particularly focusing on its safety and effectiveness. A post-hoc analysis revealed a higher mortality rate among girls who received the vaccine compared to boys, prompting further investigation into safety outcomes such as meningitis, cerebral malaria, and gender-specific mortality. These safety outcomes were graded with moderate certainty due to the rarity of such events and the wide confidence intervals observed. Multiple WHO advisory committees reviewed data from pilot implementation studies and concluded that the safety signals identified in Phase 3 trials were not causally linked to the vaccine. Additionally, these safety concerns were not observed in earlier Phase 2 trials or subsequent Phase 3 trials. The malaria vaccine pilot evaluations were designed to address outstanding safety questions. Evidence from these studies, as well as unpublished data, has been summarized in the full evidence report on the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine. The vaccine has been shown to be safe and well-tolerated, with a small risk of febrile seizures occurring within 2–3 days of vaccination. Proper planning and staff training for pharmacovigilance are recommended before vaccine introduction. Malaria remains a leading cause of childhood illness and death in sub-Saharan Africa. The introduction of the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine has been well-received by caregivers and health providers, who value its ability to reduce the severity and frequency of malaria. Positive attitudes and trust in the vaccine have grown over time, driven by its perceived health benefits for children and the broader community. Surveys and administrative data indicate that the vaccine is acceptable to the target population, with rapid scale-up achieved despite its unique dosing schedule. Importantly, the introduction of the vaccine has not negatively impacted the uptake of other childhood vaccinations, insecticide-treated net (ITN) use, or health-seeking behavior for febrile illnesses. The vaccine has extended the reach of malaria prevention tools, with more than two-thirds of children who did not sleep under an ITN receiving at least their first dose of the vaccine. Across the three pilot countries (Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi), over 90% of children now have access to at least one malaria prevention tool (ITN or RTS,S/AS01). The vaccine has demonstrated equitable uptake across socioeconomic groups and genders, with no significant variability in coverage. Mathematical models have shown that the vaccine is cost-effective in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission. At an assumed price of $5 per dose, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) was estimated at $25 per clinical case averted and $87 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted for the four-dose schedule. The public health impact and cost-effectiveness are greater in areas with higher malaria transmission, despite the higher number of doses required. The vaccine has been successfully integrated into routine immunization systems, even during the COVID-19 pandemic. Over 7 million doses have been administered across the pilot countries, with more than 650,000 children receiving their first dose. Coverage rates for the first dose exceeded 70% in all three countries, and at least 62% of children received the third dose. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of early diagnosis and prompt, effective treatment of malaria as a cornerstone of malaria control and elimination strategies. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) remain the recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria, as they are highly effective and well-tolerated. However, the emergence of artemisinin resistance in Southeast Asia poses a significant threat to global malaria control efforts. The guidelines also stress the rational use of antimalarial drugs to prevent the spread of drug resistance. Combination therapy is recommended to delay resistance and maximize treatment efficacy. Microscopy remains the field standard for malaria diagnosis, offering high sensitivity and specificity when performed by skilled technicians. It allows for species identification, parasite quantification, and monitoring of treatment responses. However, maintaining high-quality microscopy services requires significant investment in training, supervision, and infrastructure. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are an alternative diagnostic tool, particularly in settings where microscopy is not feasible. RDTs are simple to use, require minimal training, and provide rapid results, making them suitable for use in low-resource settings. However, they have limitations, such as the inability to distinguish new infections from recently treated cases when using HRP2-based tests. Despite these challenges, RDTs have expanded access to malaria diagnosis in remote and underserved areas. In summary, the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine is a safe, effective, and cost-efficient tool for malaria prevention, particularly in areas of high transmission. Its introduction has increased access to malaria prevention without negatively affecting other health interventions.
